versions.text:
The summer I turned fifteen, Grandfather was building the Linnet in his shed at Merrow Point from the plans his father drew sixty years ago. He had raced in the harbor regatta every August of his life, but his hands had grown stiff, so he taught me the steam box, and I bent each plank while he measured it. Mrs. Vale had asked to buy the boat for her grandson on her first visit to the shed. Mr. Corran, who sold us the cedar, had offered to finish it in his yard, and Grandfather had laughed.

One morning in late July the fourth plank split from end to end. Grandfather ran his thumb along the break, went to the telephone, and told Mr. Corran that a yard which sold green cedar to an old friend ought to be ashamed. He wanted a fresh board by Friday.

I spent the afternoon checking. My times at the steam box matched the ones he had taught me, and his measuring agreed with the plans to the sixteenth. I kept coming back to the window. The split plank was the only one the sun reached after noon, when the tin roof held the heat like an oven, and its twin on the shaded side, cut from the same cedar board, was as sound as the day I bent it.

“Well, Ada,” Grandfather said when I showed him, and stood at the window a long time. The next morning was fair and still, and he spent it tacking canvas over the glass and fitting a new plank. That evening Mrs. Vale came to ask whether her grandson could sail the Linnet in the regatta. I had hoped Grandfather would keep it for us, or set it aside to be rebuilt next summer, but he told her it was hers once the repair was done.

On regatta day I stood on the seawall while her grandson took the Linnet out past the moorings. I knew every plank in her, which ones I had bent and which he had, and I followed the white sail until it went behind the point, and for a while after that.

The summer I turned fifteen, Grandfather was building the Linnet in his shed at Merrow Point from the plans his father drew sixty years ago. He had raced in the harbor regatta every August of his life, but his hands had grown stiff, so he taught me the steam box, and I bent each plank while he measured it. Mr. Corran, who sold us the cedar, had offered to finish the boat in his yard, and Grandfather had laughed.

Mrs. Vale’s first visit to the shed was in June. She walked twice around the frames, asked who had drawn the lines, and said she wanted the Linnet for her grandson to sail. Grandfather told her to come back when the hull was closed. After she left he said she had a good eye, and he whistled through the rest of the day.

One morning in late July the fourth plank split from end to end. Grandfather looked at it, then at me. “How long was it in the box, Ada?” For the rest of that week he did the steaming himself, standing over the box in the heat with his watch in his hand, and he began to talk of setting the boat aside to be rebuilt next summer.

On Saturday I took the plans down to look at the fourth station. In the margin, in his father’s hand, was a note: too sharp here, eased on the first Linnet. We measured the frames again, and they matched the drawing exactly. He eased the curve where his father had eased it and repaired the plank, and when Mrs. Vale offered a fair price that evening, he told her the Linnet was spoken for. I would sail it in the regatta.

I sailed it in his old cap and came in fifth. That night I swept the shed, oiled his tools and hung them back in their places, and under his father’s note, in my smallest letters, I wrote the date and four words: he gave me this.

The summer I turned fifteen, Grandfather was building the Linnet in his shed at Merrow Point from the plans his father drew sixty years ago. He had raced in the harbor regatta every August of his life, but his hands had grown stiff. Mrs. Vale had asked to buy the boat for her grandson to sail on her first visit to the shed, and Mr. Corran, who sold us the cedar, had offered to finish it in his yard. Grandfather had laughed.

So in June he taught me the steam box. An hour for every inch of thickness, he said, then out with gloves on and onto the frames before you can count twenty, because the wood remembers being a tree. He made me bend scrap until I could do it without his hand on mine, and after that I bent each plank while he measured it.

One morning in late July the fourth plank split from end to end. “That’s the heat, Ada,” Grandfather said. He propped both doors open, hung wet sacks over the window, and said the tin roof had baked the plank before it could settle. He began to talk of setting the boat aside to be rebuilt next summer, in the cool of spring.

Two nights later, with the sacks still wet and the shed as cool as a cellar, the plank beside it split too. Both had come from the last load of cedar Mr. Corran sold us, and when I sawed the board’s end it was dark and damp at the heart. Mrs. Vale heard and asked for her money back. Grandfather rowed across, and by noon Mr. Corran’s men were towing the Linnet over to be repaired and finished in his yard, with a fair wind behind them.

I stayed in the shed. The man who had sold us wet cedar would put his own brass plate on her transom, and at the regatta people would say what a fine boat Corran’s yard had built. I swept up the shavings of every plank I had bent, and when his son waved from the towline, I kept both hands on the broom.

The summer I turned fifteen, Grandfather was building the Linnet in his shed at Merrow Point from the plans his father drew sixty years ago. He had raced in the harbor regatta every August of his life, but his hands had grown stiff, so he taught me the steam box, and I bent each plank while he measured it. Mrs. Vale had asked to buy the boat for her grandson to sail on her first visit to the shed.

In July Mr. Corran, who sold us the cedar, rowed across the harbor to look at the hull. He watched Grandfather try to hold a pencil, and then he made his offer: he would finish the Linnet in his yard in time for the regatta and charge only for the varnish. Grandfather said he would think it over, which in our family can mean anything.

One morning a week later the fourth plank split from end to end. Grandfather held his hands up to the light as if they belonged to someone else. “I marked that bevel wrong, Ada,” he said, and he spent the afternoon measuring every frame again, finding each one where the plans put it, while I stood by the steam box and said nothing.

That evening I opened my steam log. On the day I bent the fourth plank he had gone a fair distance up the coast to see Mrs. Vale, and I had pulled the plank out after forty minutes instead of an hour, wanting it on before he came home. I showed him the page. He read it twice. Then he said a repaired plank in a hurried hull would split again in the first heat of August, and that next summer the two of us would rebuild the Linnet properly. The regatta would have to manage without her.

Mrs. Vale found another boat for her grandson, and Grandfather says next summer the way other people say tomorrow. I watched him fumble the latch on the shed door that night, three tries before it caught, and in my room I counted the months to June, and then counted them again.

The summer I turned fifteen, Grandfather was building the Linnet in his shed at Merrow Point. He had raced in the harbor regatta every August of his life, but his hands had grown stiff, so he taught me the steam box, and I bent each plank while he measured it. Mrs. Vale had asked to buy the boat for her grandson to sail on her first visit to the shed. Mr. Corran, who sold us the cedar, had offered to finish it in his yard, and Grandfather had laughed.

The plans hung above the bench. His father drew them one winter at the kitchen table, with a ruler cut from a broken oar, and every Linnet since had come from those sheets. The margins were crowded with notes in two hands, his father’s upright and his own leaning, and he touched them in passing, the way people touch a doorframe.

One morning in late July the fourth plank split from end to end. Grandfather took the plans down and spread them on the bench. “He always drew her too sharp in the bow, Ada,” he said, and for two days, in the heat of the shed, he went over his father’s lines with a magnifying glass. I asked whether we should set the boat aside to be rebuilt next summer, and he kept reading.

On the third day I held the tape while he measured the frames again. At the fourth station his own pencil mark sat a quarter inch from the line on the drawing. He looked at it a while, rolled the plans up, and repaired the plank that afternoon. When Mrs. Vale asked again to buy it, he said he would race the Linnet himself. He had been a fair sailor once, and he meant to find out whether he still was.

On regatta day he took her out with his stiff hands taped and handled the tiller like a young man. He came in sixth of eleven. I watched every tack from the seawall, and that winter I practiced his bowline until I could tie it the way he does, with my eyes closed.
